example.problem: Write the year 2026 as a Roman numeral.
steps: Start with the thousands: 1000 (M) fits twice into 2026, so write MM. Remainder: 26.
Next the tens: 10 (X) fits twice into 26, so write XX. Remainder: 6.
Now 5 (V) fits once into 6, so write V. Remainder: 1.
Finally 1 (I) fits once, so write I. Remainder: 0.
Reading the symbols left to right: MMXXVI.
example.title: Writing the year 2026

faqs.a: The Romans had no symbol for zero — their system was built for counting and recording, not for arithmetic. The idea of zero as a number arrived in Europe more than a thousand years later.
faqs.q: Why is there no zero in Roman numerals?

faqs.a: MMXXVI. That is 1000 + 1000 + 10 + 10 + 5 + 1, which adds up to 2026.
faqs.q: How do you write 2026 in Roman numerals?

faqs.a: In the standard form, 3999, written MMMCMXCIX. That is 1000 + 1000 + 1000 + 900 + 90 + 9.
faqs.q: What is the largest number you can write?

faqs.a: Subtractive notation keeps numerals short: IV instead of IIII, IX instead of VIIII. Curiously, many clock faces still use IIII for 4 — a tradition that predates the standardised rules.
faqs.q: Why is 4 written as IV and not IIII?

formula.expr: Larger values first are added: XVI = 10 + 5 + 1 = 16
formula.label: Additive rule

formula.expr: A smaller value before a larger one is subtracted: IV = 5 − 1 = 4
formula.label: Subtractive rule

howItWorks: To turn a number into Roman numerals we work greedily from the largest value down. The calculator takes the biggest Roman value that fits into the number, writes its symbol, subtracts it, and repeats with the remainder. Because the table includes the subtractive pairs (CM, CD, XC, XL, IX, IV), the greedy choice always produces the correct standard form — for example 2026 becomes MM, then XX, then V, then I.

To read a Roman numeral we replace every symbol with its value and scan left to right. Whenever a smaller value sits directly before a larger one, the pair is subtractive: the smaller value is taken away from the larger one. Everything else is added. Before any of that, the input is checked against the rules of proper form, so things like IIII or VV are rejected with an explanation instead of silently giving a wrong answer.
intro: Convert any whole number from 1 to 3,999 into Roman numerals, or turn a Roman numeral back into the number it stands for. Pick the direction you need, type your value, and see every step of the conversion.

mistakes.text: The standard form uses subtraction: 4 is IV, 9 is IX, 40 is XL. Only I, X and C can be used subtractively, and only once, placed before one of the next two higher values.
mistakes.title: Writing IIII for 4

mistakes.text: Order decides the meaning: IX is 9 (10 − 1) but XI is 11 (10 + 1). A smaller value subtracts only when it comes directly before the larger one.
mistakes.title: Putting the small symbol on the wrong side

mistakes.text: The 5-based symbols are never repeated. VV is not 10 — write X. Likewise LL is wrong for 100; write C.
mistakes.title: Repeating V, L or D

mistakes.text: Standard Roman numerals stop at 3999 (MMMCMXCIX). Larger values need the overline notation, where a bar multiplies a symbol by 1000, which this calculator does not cover.
mistakes.title: Expecting numerals above 3999
